argument: The episode reads Crime and Punishment as Dostoevsky's real-world test of Russian Nihilism, where the double murder is secondary to the true drama: Raskolnikov's slow, painful coming to terms with the real reasons he killed. Against the popular claim that he embodies Nietzsche's philosophy, the episode argues Raskolnikov is a passive, reactive vessel of his era's fashionable ideas, the exact type Nietzsche critiqued, whose 'new word' merely recreates morality rather than transcending it. His utilitarian justification collapses on two fronts, an unpredictable world that defeats the calculation and a rational egoism that makes him the self-certifying arbiter of what is right, and his post-murder torment reveals he was always still a member of the moral network he thought he stood outside of. Sonya's consenting, life-affirming self-sacrifice models the alternative, and since absolution requires submitting to the legitimacy of an authority that can truly punish, confession rather than mere legal punishment is Raskolnikov's only way out of his guilt.
keyIdeas: The murder is secondary to the book's main point: the true drama is Raskolnikov's internal experience, and the killing is a perfect site for exposing the contradictions of Russian Nihilism carried out in the real world.

Raskolnikov is not an embodiment of Nietzsche's philosophy: beyond Crime and Punishment predating 'God is dead' by sixteen years, he is a reactionary, passive vessel of his era's ideas whose 'new word' recreates moral criteria, whereas the ubermensch would transcend moralizing altogether and act only from their own will.

Dostoevsky finds two connected problems in the murder's justification: a utilitarian calculus that presumes you can weigh consequences in a world you cannot fully predict, and a rational egoism that installs Raskolnikov himself as the arbiter of what is objectively right, a self-certifying move Porfiry exposes by asking who decides whether he is really special.

Raskolnikov's guilt, sickness, and nightmares show he never actually believed his rationalization: despite his theories he remains co-constituted by the relational network of ideas, people, and culture he claimed to stand outside of, which is why calling his morality 'different' only makes sense relative to that very culture.

Sonya's reply about her siblings shows a self-sacrifice that consents to her place in a network of people who need her and is life-affirming rather than renunciative, and because absolution requires believing in the legitimacy of an authority that can truly punish, only confession, not jail time alone, can free Raskolnikov from his guilt.

terms.def: The fashionable movement of Dostoevsky's time combining utilitarian moral calculation with rational egoism, whose contradictions the novel puts into practice through Raskolnikov's crime.
The assumption that an individual can not only calculate the objectively right thing to do but should also be the arbiter of that choice, placing himself at the center of the decision-making process.
Raskolnikov's term for what special people like Napoleon or Muhammad create when they go against the traditional moral order: a new set of moral criteria to live by.
Nietzsche's figure who, rather than recreating morality in their own image, has transcended the concept of morality itself and acts only on what corresponds to their own will.
The web of ideas, people, and things that co-constitutes what we are, which Raskolnikov denies his place in and which his guilt proves he never actually left.
The act that lets Raskolnikov meet the limits of his own ego and, by submitting to the legitimacy of an authority that can truly punish and absolve, opens a way out of his guilt.

anchors: the true drama of Crime and Punishment is actually the complexity of the internal experience of Raskolnikov, and him coming to terms, slowly, and painfully, with the true reasons why he committed the murders in the first place
Cause Raskolnikov was the exact kind of person that Nietzsche spent most of his career critiquing.

Nietzsche’s ubermensch then is not someone that recreates morality in their own image, like Raskolnikov, the ubermensch, if this is someone who can exist, would have, in a sense, transcended the very concept of morality itself

And the second big problem stems right out of that one–it’s the rational egoism that often accompanies this Russian Nihilism, that magically places Raskolnikov at the center of this decision-making process.
he didn’t actually kill those people for utilitarian reasons, he did it as a type of ego-driven fantasy, where he wanted to run a test to see if he was special, if he was truly different
What if you’re not very special, and that’s exactly what makes you think you’re more special than you are? Real question: who’s the governing body that gets to decide that… just you?
